\section[meditar]{meditar — to meditate; to ponder}

\label{lesson:ES-C767-meditar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the achievement, then the Spanish for talent.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: meditar}
\textbf{meditar} — \textquotedblleft{}to meditate; to ponder\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Medito diez minutos cada mañana.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I meditate for ten minutes every morning.}
\end{quote}

Also to think something over: \emph{meditar una decisión}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{meditar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{meditārī} \textquotedblleft{}to think over, to practise\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\end{itemize}

\section[la meditación]{la meditación — meditation}

\label{lesson:ES-C767-meditacion}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for talent, then the Spanish for to meditate.

\textbf{la meditación} — \textquotedblleft{}meditation\textquotedblright{}.

\section[la voluntad]{la voluntad — will, willpower}

\label{lesson:ES-C767-voluntad}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to meditate, then the Spanish for meditation.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la voluntad}
\textbf{la voluntad} — \textquotedblleft{}will, willpower\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Con fuerza de voluntad, todo es posible.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{With willpower, anything is possible.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Fuerza de voluntad} — willpower. \emph{Buena voluntad} — goodwill.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{voluntad} is usually traced to Latin \emph{voluntās}, \emph{voluntātem} \textquotedblleft{}will\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{velle} \textquotedblleft{}to want\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.

\section[estirarse]{estirarse — to stretch}

\label{lesson:ES-C767-estirarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for meditation, then the Spanish for will.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: estirarse}
\textbf{estirarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to stretch\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Me estiro antes de correr.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I stretch before running.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Estirar las piernas} — to stretch your legs.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{estirarse} is built on \emph{tirar} \textquotedblleft{}to pull\textquotedblright{} with the prefix \emph{es-}. For \emph{tirar} the origin is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[el masaje]{el masaje — the massage}

\label{lesson:ES-C767-masaje}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for will, then the Spanish for to stretch.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el masaje}
\textbf{el masaje} — \textquotedblleft{}the massage\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Después del partido me dieron un masaje.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{After the match I had a massage.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Dar un masaje} — to give a massage.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{masaje} was borrowed from French \emph{massage} (EtymDB), from \emph{masser} \textquotedblleft{}to knead\textquotedblright{}. Beyond French the origin is not settled; Arabic and Greek sources have both been proposed.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[(dialogue)]{How it was — back to the first story of a trip}

\label{lesson:ES-R767-repaso-como-fue}



\begin{quote}
From the first chapter about experiences: say the Spanish for \textquotedblleft{}happy\textquotedblright{} and for \textquotedblleft{}during, for\textquotedblright{}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the scene, then the events: \emph{Llovía. Llegamos a la playa y luego comimos.}
  \item how long: \emph{Estuvimos allí durante una semana.}
  \item \emph{feliz} for him and for her, the same word: \emph{Él estaba feliz. Ella estaba feliz.}
  \item a comparison: \emph{Este viaje me gustó más que el otro.}
  \item what you hope for next: \emph{Espero volver el año que viene.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In your story, which tense set the scene? (The imperfect: \emph{llovía}.) Which told the events? (The preterite: \emph{llegamos}, \emph{comimos}.) Why does \emph{feliz} not change for \emph{ella}? (It ends in a consonant.) What two things can \emph{esperar} mean? (To wait and to hope.)
\end{tcolorbox}
